editorials.title: Perilous retreat: On gram sabhas, tribal land issues
editorials.passage:
Tribal organisations should recognise the Indian state’s attempt to lower the legal barriers erected by the Forest Rights Act (FRA) as a threat to their survival. The Committee on Public Undertakings’ suggestion that a project require the consent of only most, rather than all, gram sabhas affected by that project, as the FRA intends in spirit , portends a significant jurisprudential change. A regime that deems the acquiescence of 70%-75% of affected gram sabhas to suffice will reduce gram sabhas from democratic bodies protecting the constitutional rights of its specific inhabitants to corporate stakeholders. If the rule enters force, a project developer may bypass the consent of a village located directly within a proposed reservoir, say, while ensuring that less affected villages have provided their no-objection certificates. The matter is of a piece with the political fight over classifying tribal communities: by altering the demographic composition of who qualifies as a community member, the state will have an easier time splitting a village assembly and engineering consent. The refusal of the Tribal Affairs Ministry to claim jurisdiction over this issue creates a dangerous regulatory vacuum that leaves the Centre and State governments unchecked to rewrite the rules by which forested land is diverted for non-forest use. While the FRA does not include a clause requiring a no-objection certificate from every affected gram sabha, it is untrue that there is at present no legal requirement that gram sabha decisions can be bypassed.

The government has been rapidly scaling up energy infrastructure, including the long-stalled Teesta-IV project, to meet macroeconomic goals while, in a previous avatar, having passed the FRA to undo “historical injustices” meted out to forest-dependent communities. But the path the state seems willing to pursue, hewing to the notion that the consent requirement was never part of the FRA, is plainly ignoble. If the Environment Ministry entertains the idea, it must change the relevant rules or legislation openly and democratically. The Tribal Affairs Ministry resorting to a technicality, between the FRA and the Environment Ministry’s rules, to recuse itself is hardly better as the bureaucratic manoeuvre could strip forest-dependent communities of their most potent legal instrument. The foundation of these communities’ livelihoods, culture, identity, and political autonomy is land, so they have fought to resist displacement and dispossession and to secure customary collective ownership. In recognition of the social and environment services ST communities continue to render in India and their contribution to national development, including helping meet India’s climate commitments, the Centre and States must also strengthen the powers conferred by the Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement and Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Acts to gram sabhas in Scheduled Areas.

editorials.title: Falling edifice: On the Delhi private hostel building collapse
editorials.passage:
The collapse of a five-storey building in Delhi , being run as a private hostel that killed seven and injured five in a densely populated colony abutting Delhi University’s South Campus, has brought to light the twin issues of haphazard development in the capital city’s residential areas and the shortage of affordable housing for students . With over 70,000 students entering Delhi University every year and almost half of them needing accommodation on a student budget, the city has failed to keep up with the growing demand. The University has, for all practical purposes, absolved itself of the responsibility, citing lack of land, leaving private players to cash in and run paying guest accommodations or private hostels that are not regulated. In a setup where every extra bed means more revenue, matchbox-sized rooms, often located in buildings that flout building bylaws and fire safety regulations and have no ventilation, are what several students call home. As soon as they arrive in the capital, students from many parts of the country realise that they are paying to live in the city not just in monetary terms but with their safety, security and sanity.

The Delhi government says that it wants the city to be a national education hub and harness the soft power of its youth, but that will be not possible without addressing the need for affordable, safe student housing. The Delhi government has suspended five senior officers of the civic body, ordered a probe and announced that it was working on introducing a stringent policy under which every building used for public activity would be required to undergo periodic structural audits and obtain safety certifications. It must go beyond these reactive measures to seek more durable solutions. In 2024, the basement of a coaching centre flooded due to heavy rains claiming the lives of three civil service aspirants. After that incident as well, probes were ordered, basements were sealed and legal action was taken against owners but a larger systemic change remains elusive. The Centre and the Government of NCT must work together with educational institutions to develop more residential, travel and learning facilities for students. The introduction of four-year undergraduate programmes also means that students will stay on for an additional year, increasing the pressure on accommodation. Private hostels can be part of the solution, but crumbling civic infrastructure, illegal construction and lack of safety audits must be tackled through policy and strict enforcement.

editorials.title: Schedule Test matches at traditional venues
editorials.passage: On Sunday morning, when it was known that East Zone’s Vaibhav Sooryavanshi would be batting first in the Duleep Trophy final against South Zone in Chennai, fans made a beeline for M A Chidambaram Stadium. The turnout validated the Board of Control for Cricket in India’s choice in more than one way. First, it was right to host the final in front of fans. When the schedule was out initially, the final was supposed to be a closed-doors affair (barring some journalists) at the BCCI’s Centre of Excellence outside Bengaluru. But the final of the 65-year-old tournament ought to be celebrated in front of fans. The BCCI also deserves appreciation for ensuring domestic red-ball cricket featuring big players—in the ongoing final, as many as seven of the 22 players have earned India caps. Out of the seven, Sooryavanshi is one of the hottest properties in world cricket. Beyond him, Ishan Kishan, Tilak Varma and Mohammed Siraj won the T20 World Cup, while Mohammed Shami is a stalwart in his own right. Then there is Devdutt Padikkal, who could be India’s No 3 Test batter for years to come. The next rung features the 23-year-old Ravichandran Smaran, who is vying for an India cap.With free entry, over 10,000 spectators turned up on the opening day. It begs the question what’s stopping the BCCI from allotting Chennai one Test match per year? It’s time to reopen the debate for a city that used to host mid-January Pongal Tests for decades up to 1988. It’s a good idea to spread the game’s longest format to other parts, but also it’s increasingly clear that traditional centres like Kolkata, Mumbai, Chennai and Bengaluru attract much larger Test crowds than others..Virat Kohli’s wish, expressed almost a decade ago, of playing in fixed Test centres is yet to be acted upon. This would face two purposes with a straight bat—ensuring an appreciative atmosphere and helping the team get acclimatised to certain conditions. This is why England, South Africa and Australia pick set venues. But as the BCCI sticks to its rotation policy for now, it is risking demoralising players in front of empty stands. editorials.title: Court order underlines duty of restraint in applying Executive power
editorials.passage: Power must answer to the law. That is the larger significance of the Allahabad High Court’s criticism of the Gautam Buddha Nagar administration over the preventive detention of student-activist Akriti Chaudhary. The immediate issue is the invocation of the National Security Act without, in the court’s assessment, sufficient material to justify so grave a curtailment of liberty. The court’s observations on the administration were unusually strong, describing its conduct as an “Orwellian dystopia”. The remark is a reminder of the responsibility that accompanies the considerable powers vested in a district magistrate.Chaudhary’s case is part of the larger story of protests over paper leaks, amid growing disquiet among students including over the offhand “cockroach” remark. The July protests were followed by allegations of excessive police force. The Supreme Court subsequently intervened and directed the withdrawal of FIRs against the students.The episode raises a larger question about the manner in which State power is exercised when citizens challenge authority. Laws such as the NSA confer extraordinary powers on the Executive precisely because circumstances may sometimes demand exceptional action. But the greater the power, the greater the obligation to establish that its use is necessary and proportionate. It therefore demands the highest degree of scrutiny and restraint..This is also why institutional checks matter. The Executive, Legislature and Judiciary have distinct constitutional roles, but none exists in isolation from the larger constitutional framework. When one institution has to step in to correct the lapses of another, the objective should not be to establish institutional superiority. It should be to restore the balance that protects the citizen.The Judiciary has given important directions in the cases arising from the student protests, and its strong observations should not be dismissed merely as rhetoric. The capacity for reflection must extend to every institution. As Chief Justice Surya Kant has said, “Judges, like the institutions they lead, remain capable of growth, correction and improvement.”That principle applies to all institutions entrusted with public power. Their authority derives ultimately from the Constitution and is sustained by the manner in which the authority is exercised. The citizen, particularly when challenging authority, must not become more vulnerable because the State possesses greater power. editorials.title: Quick Take | Nation of loud mobs
editorials.passage: Sunday's deadly assault on 54-year-old guitarist Chongtham Vikram Singh at his own apartment in Delhi was symptomatic of three troubling phenomena increasingly rearing their ugly heads—especially in the country’s north. The first is the continuing discrimination against citizens from the Northeast, to address which the Delhi police have even set up a dedicated cell. Second, the increasing tendency of lynch mobs feeling entitled to take the law into their own hands. Such cases have spread so grotesquely that the Supreme Court in 2018 condemned them as “horrendous acts of mobocracy”. Third is the phenomenon protesting which Singh drew his neighbours’ ire—the unthinking loudness that is becoming common at festivals. Quietude should be taught as a virtue in a society unbothered about ear-splitting noise seriously distressing others..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: Growth and energy security
editorials.passage:
India's spectacular 7.8 per cent real GDP growth in Q1 FY27 deserves to be viewed in the context of the extraordinary circumstances in which it was achieved. This was a quarter marked by a severe West Asian conflict, disruption around the Strait of Hormuz, volatile crude prices and fears of an energy supply shock cascading across economies. Yet India kept moving. Factories ran. Trucks moved. Airlines flew. Restaurants remained open. Hotels functioned. Households cooked. 

Cities continued to receive gas. Most importantly, the energy shock did not become an economy-wide supply crisis. Energy security was therefore not the sole reason for India’s 7.8 per cent growth, but it was a critical shock absorber that prevented an external geopolitical crisis from becoming an internal economic crisis. The most important part of that story was the speed and breadth with which India diversified its crude procurement when the crisis erupted. India imports nearly 90 per cent of its crude requirement. The Strait of Hormuz has traditionally been a critical artery for those supplies, with roughly 45 per cent of imports transiting the route before the crisis. 

Yet within days of the disruption, India had substantially altered its sourcing map. By March 2026, around 70 per cent of India’s crude imports were arriving through routes outside Hormuz, compared with about 55 per cent earlier. India was sourcing crude from 40 countries, against 27 in 2006-07. The government also reported that the volumes exceeded what the disrupted Hormuz route would have delivered. The early weeks demonstrated the value of this strategy in hard numbers. In March, as Middle Eastern supplies plunged, Indian refiners almost doubled their Russian crude purchases, from about 1.04 million barrels per day in February to nearly 2.25 million barrels per day. 

Russian crude consequently accounted for roughly half of India’s March imports, while supplies from the Middle East fell sharply. India did not stop there. Additional supplies were secured from the UAE, Venezuela and other producers, while refiners looked beyond traditional Gulf suppliers. By May, crude imports had rebounded to 5.27 million barrels per day. Russia supplied about 1.92 million barrels per day, while UAE supplies surged 41 per cent to 942,500 barrels per day - above pre-war levels. Venezuela and Iraq also contributed to the diversified basket. 

There was another crucial element: India’s refiners were operating at very high capacity utilisation, allowing the country to convert this diversified crude supply into usable fuels even as global markets were under severe stress. The government noted that some refineries were operating above 100 per cent of nominal capacity. This was not crisis management improvised in March. It was the payoff from a decade-long strategy. India’s refiners had progressively expanded sourcing across Russia, Africa, Latin America, the United States and other producers. 

The country had also built refining capabilities capable of processing a wide variety of crude grades. For an import-dependent economy, energy security does not necessarily mean eliminating imports; it means ensuring that no single geography, supplier or shipping route can hold the economy hostage and adding to the storage capacities of oil, LPG, and LNG, etc. The Hormuz crisis put that proposition to the test and India passed it. The second test was even more intimate: the kitchen. 

India imports about 60 per cent of its LPG consumption, and approximately 90 per cent of those imports normally arrive through the Strait of Hormuz. A prolonged disruption could therefore have directly affected millions of households. The response was swift. On March 8, the government directed refineries and petrochemical complexes to maximise LPG production by diverting propane, butane, propylene and butenes into the LPG pool. Domestic LPG production increased by 25 per cent according to the government's initial assessment, and by 28 per cent within five days according to the Petroleum Minister’s subsequent parliamentary statement. 

Procurement was simultaneously diversified. LPG cargoes were secured from the United States, Norway, Canada, Algeria and Russia, alongside available Gulf supplies. The result was critical: despite the unprecedented geopolitical disruption, domestic cooking-gas supplies were protected and oil companies maintained high levels of cylinder deliveries. But the objective was larger than protecting households. Commercial LPG is the lifeblood of restaurants, hotels, dhabas, canteens, food processors and other service businesses. A prolonged shortage would have rapidly translated into higher food costs, business closures and employment disruption. 

The government therefore prioritised commercial LPG for precisely these sectors while simultaneously accelerating the transition to PNG. The PNG push may ultimately prove to be one of the most consequential aspects of the response. Under the Natural Gas Control Order issued in March, domestic PNG and CNG for transport were given 100 per cent supply protection. Gas allocation to other industrial and commercial consumers was managed according to priority. Alternative LNG procurement was also activated, with new cargoes secured through alternative sources and routes. At the same time, city-gas-distribution companies were asked to prioritise PNG connections for hotels, restaurants and canteens. States were offered additional commercial LPG allocation if they facilitated the transition from LPG to PNG. The scale was remarkable. 

By May 21, about 7.64 lakh PNG connections had been gasified since March, with infrastructure created for another 2.81 lakh. This is what distinguishes strategic crisis management from mere firefighting. India did not simply seek to survive the energy shock. It used the shock to accelerate a more resilient energy architecture. That mattered enormously for the services economy. Hotels, restaurants, canteens and other commercial establishments could continue operating even as LPG supplies came under pressure. Energy policy helped ensure that a geopolitical crisis thousands of kilometres away did not become a consumption and services crisis at home. To safeguard against global supply shocks and West Asian geopolitical tensions, India is significantly expanding its energy infrastructure. 

Under the management of state-owned Indian Strategic Petroleum Reserves Limited (ISPRL), the country is transitioning toward an integrated "Strategic Fuel System." This initiative includes a proposed $42-billion, decade-long mega-programme aimed at adding 28 million tonnes (MT) of crude, 9 MT of LNG, and 4 MT of LPG storage capacity. Investments will be channelized through Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs), and Public-Private Partnership (PPP) models. As part of this expansion, India is also collaborating with the UAE’s Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC). 

ADNOC currently leases space in India’s caverns (such as Mangaluru) and plans to scale up its storage footprint in the country to 30 million barrels, while India explores counter-storage options in Fujairah, UAE. Expanding such strategic storage options both domestically and internationally will help ensure long-term energy security. But resilience cannot be the end goal. The ultimate objective must be to reduce India’s underlying import vulnerability. This is where Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s emphasis on energy Atmanirbharta assumes strategic importance. India is now opening new frontiers of domestic exploration, particularly in deepwater areas. 

Nowhere is the opportunity more intriguing than the Andaman basin. ONGC and Oil India have undertaken ultra-deepwater exploration there, with drilling targeting depths of up to 5,000 metres. A recent well yielded traces of light crude and condensate, reservoir-quality facies and other evidence indicating an active petroleum system. Commercial accumulations, however, have not yet been established and it would be premature to declare an Andaman oil bonanza. But the strategic direction is unmistakable. India’s coastline and surrounding waters could become a much larger component of its future energy story. The Bay of Bengal, in particular, represents a frontier where energy security, maritime security and the blue economy converge. 

This is consistent with a larger vision the Prime Minister has repeatedly articulated: India must become sufficiently self-reliant in critical energy inputs so that its economic rise is not constrained by geopolitical developments elsewhere. The 7.8 per cent GDP number is therefore significant for more than its headline value. It demonstrates that India’s growth engine remained resilient when the global energy system was under extraordinary stress. Consumption remained robust. Manufacturing expanded. Services remained buoyant. Investment strengthened. And the energy system continued to supply the economy with the fuel it needed to function. 

Energy security did not create every one of those growth drivers. But it protected them. The diversification of crude imports, high refinery utilisation, rapid expansion of domestic LPG production, protection of household energy supplies, accelerated PNG adoption and the push into deepwater exploration are pieces of one larger architecture. The ultimate test of an energy strategy is not whether it works when oil flows freely and geopolitics is calm. It is whether the economy keeps moving when the world becomes uncertain. During the Hormuz crisis, India demonstrated that it could absorb an extraordinary external shock without surrendering its growth momentum. 

The next challenge is to move from resilience to Atma Nirbharta. If India can combine diversified imports with rising domestic exploration, deeper strategic reserves, greater gas penetration and new hydrocarbon discoveries, the energy sector could become not merely a shield against crises, but a powerful engine of India’s next economic surge. Energy security, in other words, is no longer simply about securing India’s energy. It is about securing India’s rise. 

(The writers are, respectively, national spokesperson of BJP and an energy professional)

editorials.title: Mountain without a border ~ II
editorials.passage:
In the same weeks that the mountain came down, India and China agreed ~ quietly, and to their credit ~ to talk to one another a little more. They would widen the military hotlines that link their commanders and convene their boundary working groups more regularly, the patient machinery by which two wary armies keep a contested frontier from tipping into accident. It is a real and welcome thing. It is also an accidental confession. We have taught the frontier to speak, soldier to soldier, about the war that will probably never come. We have left it mute about the flood that certainly will. 

That silence is the whole opportunity, and closing it asks no one to love his neighbour. It asks only that three governments admit what the water has already proved ~ that above a certain altitude they share one weather, one watershed and one set of dangers, and that meeting those dangers three times over, in three languages, from behind three closed borders, is a way of losing slowly. What the region needs is not another season of goodwill but a standing arrangement with a treaty beneath it: a Himalayan mutual-aid compact, dull enough to survive the next diplomatic freeze and precise enough to save lives in the first hours, while lives are still there to be saved. 

Its first business would be a shared pair of eyes. What matters most in these mountains is not the movement of troops but the filling of lakes and the loosening of high faces ~ and, as this collapse warned, a sensor trained on a glacial lake will not hear a bedrock failure that was never a lake. Today each state watches only its own slope and files it where the others cannot read it. A common register of dangerous lakes and unstable faces, fed by pooled satellite and ground monitoring and open to every valley downstream, is the cheapest life-saving instrument on offer and the least threatening to anyone’s sovereignty. 

A glacier does not become less Chinese for being watched by a Nepali, or less Indian for being watched by both. Eyes are worth little without a voice, so the compact’s second task is a common alarm ~ a single protocol under which a reading taken beneath one flag reaches the villages beneath another in minutes, not through the slow courtesy of diplomatic notes. Its third is the corridor: routes and altitudes agreed in advance along which a rescue helicopter, a medical team or an engineering column may cross the line in a catastrophe’s first hours without waiting for a clearance that, at the usual pace, arrives after the funerals. 

A permission settled in the calm is worth a hundred pleaded in the wreckage. Beyond the emergency lies the slower work. If we are to go on damming these rivers ~ and we will ~ then the three of us who dam them ought to agree on how, adopting common resilience standards for where a powerhouse may sit above a known hazard and how it must be built to outlast one, with inspection that does not stop politely at the border. Heavy bridging and earth-moving plant could be pooled and pre-positioned rather than flown in piecemeal after each collapse. And when the water has done its worst, the country it strikes should not be left alone with the bill: a regional reconstructionfinance facility, paid into in the quiet years and drawn upon in the ruinous ones, would spread the cost that now falls, by the accident of where a glacier sat, on whichever economy stood beneath it. 

Such a fund should teach as well as console ~ its money moving only where the corridor is opened and the new standard met, so that a plant rebuilt to the old drawing draws no second cheque while a village moved off the debris path does. To all of which the seasoned objection is ready, and it is not a foolish one. You cannot, it runs, build shared institutions across a border that is itself unsettled. Let a foreign team cross the line, even to save lives, and you have conceded something about whose line it is; sit at a table apportioning a common watershed and you have dignified the other man's claim to half of it. In a region where the boundary is the quarrel, cooperation can look like surrender. The answer is that the compact is built to prejudge precisely nothing, and that neighbours far more hostile than these three have already done exactly this. 

Watching a glacier together draws no line on any map; a rescue corridor confers no right of way a court could one day cite. India and Pakistan ran a shared river commission through two wars without settling Kashmir, and opened crossing points along the Line of Control to move earthquake relief in 2005 on the plain understanding that a gate is not a boundary. But those arrangements show why goodwill alone will not do: the flood-season river readings China shares with India were quietly withheld during the standoff of 2017, and a courtesy can always be withdrawn. A treaty obligation, precisely because it is walled off from the weather of the frontier, cannot. 

If corps commanders can keep a hotline open without prejudice to sovereignty, dam engineers can surely keep a shared inventory of lakes. None of this need wait on a grand ratification no legislature will grant in a single grieving season. It can begin with memoranda formalising what the rescue is already improvising at the disaster’s face, and let the binding treaty be the destination, not the first step; grief opens windows that calmer seasons close, and this one should be used. Nor is any of it only a matter of foreign policy. The same discipline the compact would demand abroad is the discipline we have postponed at home. To adopt common standards for the high Himalaya is to be forced, at last, to look honestly at what we have already built and are still building in Himachal, in Sikkim, in Jammu and Kashmir. 

A relook is not a moratorium dressed as virtue; it is the plain work of re-grading each project against slope failure and debris pulse, not merely against the rainfall year some consultant once used. Some will pass. Some will need redesign. A few should be left on paper. That is not a concession wrung from us by neighbours; it is a reckoning we owe ourselves, and have deferred for as long as the projects kept the lights on. None of this asks the three governments to trust one another. 

It asks only that they act on a fact they already share and mostly ignore. The frontier we have just taught to speak of armies still has nothing to say about ice, and the ice is the likelier killer. The convoy will always be needed; grief will always find work. But a region that can keep a hotline open against a war it dreads can surely keep one open against a flood it knows is coming ~ and the honest measure of whether we have understood this August at all will be whether, when the next mountain lets go, the warning crosses the border before the water does.


(The writer is a practising Chartered Accountant. He can be reached at kannan@cakt.in)

editorials.title: Priorities for WB’s ailing health system
editorials.passage:
Having assumed office, the new health minister, Dr Sarwadwat Mukherjee is making sincere efforts to improve the health system in West Bengal. He has made substantial progress in expanding access to healthcare over the past few months. A large proportion of government healthcare services are provided free of cost, making the public health system the principal source of treatment for economically vulnerable families through Ayushman/Mukhyamantri health scheme. 

However, expansion of infrastructure alone cannot guarantee a high-quality health system. The next phase of reform must focus on quality, human resources, accountability, safety and public trust. Recent assessments of West Bengal's public health infrastructure have highlighted significant shortages of specialist doctors, nurses, paramedical personnel and essential medicines. The CAG's performance audit of public health infrastructure identified serious gaps in manpower, infrastructure and service delivery. Strengthening the system therefore requires not merely constructing more hospitals, but ensuring that existing institutions are adequately staffed, equipped and efficiently managed. The f irst priority should b e strengthening primary healthcare. 

A well-functioning network of primary health centres and community-level facilities can diagnose and treat common illnesses before they become medical emergencies. Properly equipped primary care facilities can also reduce the overwhelming patient load on medical colleges and tertiary hospitals. Every major health centre should have adequate doctors, nurses, diagnostic facilities, essential medicines and reliable referral and ambulance services. The second major priority is human resource planning. West Bengal needs sustained recruitment of doctors, nurses, lab oratory technicians, pharmacists and other healthcare professionals. 

Vacancies should be filled transparently and postings in rural and underserved areas should be supported by appropriate financial incentives, accommodation, career advancement and professional development opportunities. Equally important is improving the working environment so that talented healthcare professionals remain within the public system. Patient safety and hospital quality must become measurable objectives. Government hospitals should adopt regular clinical audits, infection-control programmes, mortality reviews and independent quality assessments. 

Digital hospital management systems can improve monitoring of bed availability, medicine stocks, diagnostic services and waiting times. However, technology should complement, not replace, responsible clinical and administrative leadership. Another urgent concern is the safety of doctors and healthcare workers. Violence against doctors, nurses and hospital staff damages morale and ultimately harms patients. Every major government hospital should have trained security personnel, functional surveillance systems and rapid response mechanisms for potentially violent situations. 

At the same time, better communication with patients and families, transparent information about treatment and waiting times, and effective grievance redressal systems can prevent many conflicts before they escalate. A substantial and sustained increase in health expenditure is equally important. The 2026-27 West Bengal budget has increased the allocation for Health and Family Welfare, but the crucial issue is how effectively these resources are converted into better services and outcomes. Investment should give priority to manpower, essential medicines, diagnostics, critical-care capacity, maintenance of existing facilities and primary healthcare, not only new buildings. 

The availability of essential medicines and diagnostics should be guaranteed throughout the year. Stock-outs force poor patients to purchase costly medicines from the market, defeating the purpose of free public healthcare. A transparent, technology-supported procurement and supply-chain system, with real time monitoring of drug inventories, could substantially improve reliability. Finally, healthcare reform must be based on accountability and public trust. Hospitals should be assessed not simply by the number of patients treated or beds created, but by outcomes: mortality rates, infection rates, patient satisfaction, waiting time, availability of medicines and referral efficiency. 

The department’s recent emphasis on hospital monitoring from Swastha Bhaban by videography provides an opportunity to strengthen lacunae in administration, provided monitoring is linked to corrective action and professional accountability. West Bengal has the infrastructure, medical expertise and institutional base to build a stronger health system. The challenge now is to move from mindless expansion to excellence. Greater investment, adequate manpower, secure workplaces, reliable medicines, strong primary care and transparent accountability can together create a healthcare system that is not only accessible, but also safe, efficient and worthy of public confidence. 

(The writer is ex-consultant specialist, SSKM hospital & IPGMER, Kolkata)

editorials.title: Demographic Deadline
editorials.passage:
For decades, India worried about having too many people. Population control, family planning and the spectre of unchecked demographic growth shaped public policy and political debate. Now the country confronts a reversal that should provoke not panic, but serious thought: India's fertility rate has fallen below the replacement level of 2.1 children per woman. The significance lies not in an imminent population collapse. India will continue growing for some time because of demographic momentum. Nor should falling fertility automatically be treated as a national failure. 

On the contrary, it reflects profound social change: women are marrying later, receiving more education and exercising greater control over reproduction; families are responding rationally to the rising costs of raising children. The real question is whether India’s institutions have kept pace with this transformation. India’s demographic dividend ~ the economic advantage supposedly conferred by a large working-age population ~ was always presented as a historic opportunity. But a demographic dividend is not a gift. Young people become an economic asset only when they are healthy, educated and productively employed. Otherwise, a large youth population can become a source of frustration rather than prosperity. That makes declining fertility a deadline. 

India has a limited period in which an exceptionally large working-age population will support relatively fewer elderly dependants. If the country fails to generate productive employment, improve education and bring more women into the workforce during this window, it cannot assume that another generation will provide a second opportunity. The challenge is complicated by India’s enormous internal demographic differences. Bihar and Uttar Pradesh remain substantially younger than southern and eastern states where fertility has fallen sharply. Kerala and Tamil Nadu are already confronting questions associated with ageing societies, while other parts of the country continue to grapple with a rapidly expanding young population. 

This divergence also has political consequences. The proposed delimitation of parliamentary constituencies has exposed an uncomfortable contradiction in Indian federalism: states that successfully controlled population growth fear being penalised with diminished political representation, while faster-growing states could gain more seats. A demographic achievement in one generation may thus become a political disadvantage in the next. Yet the worst response would be to imitate countries that have reacted to low fertility with nationalist anxiety and exhortations for women to have more children. India should resist the temptation to make reproduction a new instrument of public policy. 

The more urgent task is to prepare for the society that demographic change is already creating: an economy requiring higher productivity rather than merely more workers; cities capable of supporting smaller families and an ageing population; workplaces that enable women to combine careers and motherhood; and social-security systems that do not depend indefinitely on ever-larger younger generations. India’s demographic revolution should therefore be understood neither as catastrophe nor celebration. It is a transition that imposes a timetable on the country’s economic ambitions. The question is no longer how many Indians the future will produce. It is whether India can make the most of those it already has.

editorials.title: Legal Frontiers
editorials.passage:
Great-power rivalry is usually measured in aircraft carriers, tariffs and missiles. Increasingly, however, one of its most consequential battlefields lies elsewhere: in statutes, courtrooms and corporate compliance departments. China’s growing embrace of extraterritorial law marks a significant shift in the character of its competition with the United States. 

For decades, Beijing has condemned Washington’s ability to extend its influence beyond American territory through sanctions, export controls and the global reach of the dollar-based financial system. Now China is developing legal instruments of its own to resist such pressure ~ and, increasingly, to impose pressure in return. The implications extend well beyond diplomatic disputes. A multinational company operating simultaneously in China and the United States may increasingly find itself confronted with incompatible legal commands. Washington may demand that it sever ties with a sanctioned Chinese entity. 

Beijing may regard compliance with that demand as participation in illegitimate foreign interference. Obeying one government can therefore expose the company to punishment by another. This is qualitatively different from an ordinary trade war. Tariffs raise the cost of doing business; conflicting legal obligations can make it impossible to determine what lawful business actually means. China’s recent strengthening of its anti-sanctions and anti-extraterritorial framework reflects a broader strategic calculation. Beijing cannot yet replicate America’s financial power. 

The renminbi does not command the international position of the dollar, and Chinese banks lack the same centrality to global commerce. But China possesses another formidable source of leverage: access to one of the world’s largest markets. The message to foreign companies is becoming increasingly clear. Commercial access may carry political and legal obligations. The underlying principle is consequential: borders need not limit a state’s legal interests. There is a historical irony here. China’s Communist Party has long invoked the humiliations of the nineteenth century, when foreign powers secured extraordinary legal privileges on Chinese territory and placed themselves partly beyond Chinese jurisdiction. Extraterritoriality became synonymous with national weakness and foreign domination. Yet power changes one’s view of legal principles. 

A China strong enough to challenge the international order is discovering that law, like finance and technology, can be used as an instrument of statecraft. The danger is not simply that Beijing is copying Washington. It is that two great powers are establishing overlapping systems of legal coercion. Other countries and multinational corporations will increasingly be forced to navigate between them, choosing whose sanctions to respect, whose technologies to use and whose political sensitivities to accommodate. 

Globalisation was once expected to make borders progressively less important. The opposite may now be happening. Borders remain physically intact, but national laws are reaching farther across them. The emerging world order may therefore be defined not by a single global rulebook but by competing legal spheres of influence. The decisive question for businesses may no longer be where they operate. It may be which sovereign power they can afford to disobey

editorials.title: Sleight of hand
editorials.passage:
The legislation that brought into being the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme was perhaps the most significant one in the entire history of post-Independence India. It rectified, no doubt to a very limited extent, a basic lacuna of the Indian Constitution: while the Constitution gave to every citizen a set of civil and political rights, it did not provide any fundamental economic rights.

The MGNREGS, by contrast, gave every rural household the right to demand and obtain up to 100 days of employment per year; if employment was not provided within 15 days of demanding it, then the member of the household demanding work had to be compensated. This right was universal in a dual sense: it was neither targeted, nor confined to particular regions of the country. True, its coverage that extended to only 100 days of employment per household was a major limitation; nonetheless, the MGNREGS proved to be a lifeline for workers in rural India. In periods of crisis in particular, such as during the pandemic when millions of workers had to trudge back from the towns where they normally worked to their villages, the MGNREGS proved to be an invaluable source of support.

It was introduced in Parliament on December 21, 2004, and passed unanimously on August 23, 2005. It came into effect on February 2, 2006, after considerable discussion in the House and the media, and after a Parliamentary Standing Committee had collected evidence over months from a large number of persons and fine-tuned it. The fact that its adoption was unanimous and followed such meticulous scrutiny had lulled many, including this writer, into believing that, although not the result of a formal constitutional amendment, it enjoyed a quasi-constitutional status, which placed it beyond any kind of modification by a mere parliamentary majority.

We had, however, grossly underestimated the extraordinary meanness of the current National Democratic Alliance government, which has now abrogated the MGNREGA and replaced it by Viksit Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin). This new legislation, VB-G RAM G, was introduced on December 16, 2025, passed by Parliament on December 18 and 19 and came into effect on July 1, 2026. The extremely brief interval between its introduction in Parliament and its passing, in contrast to MGNREGS where the interval was eight months, shows the totally cavalier manner in which it has come into being: the objective seems to have been more to scuttle the MGNREGS than to improve upon it through Parliament’s collective application of the mind.

This new legislation differs from the MGNREGS in at least three crucial ways: first, under the earlier Act anybody anywhere could demand work and work had to be provided within 15 days, failing which the person was entitled to compensation; under the VB-G RAM G, however, the areas where the scheme would be operative were to be notified by the Central government from time to time which ends the demand-driven nature of the scheme and hence any right to employment.

Two, the MGNREGS was a virtually fully-funded scheme of the Central government. The entire wage bill of the unskilled workers and 75% of total material costs were borne by the Central government with state governments meeting 25% of material costs. On average, the state governments’ share came to approximately 10% of the total costs under the MGNREGS. Now, under the VB-G RAM G, the Central government has unilaterally jacked up the state governments' share to 40%. Given the much tighter fiscal constraints that state governments face, raising their share to 40% is both a means of cutting down the operation of the scheme and putting the blame for it on state governments, particularly in states not ruled by the NDA where the fiscal constraint is tighter.

Third, there is centralization of decision-making power; decisions earlier left to gram sabhas and state governments are now to be taken by the Central government. In effect, therefore, the Centre wants to control the rural employment scheme while paying less for it.

Government propaganda predictably has been trying to pass off the VB-G RAM G as a better employment scheme than the MGNREGS since it offers employment for up to 125 days compared to the 100 days under the MGNREGS; but what it glosses over is that 100 days of employment were offered earlier wherever and whenever there was demand for employment, while now the offer of 125 days would be confined only to pockets determined by the Central government. In effect, VB-G RAM G would be used by the Central government to fund its own schemes in rural areas, while offloading a large part of the financial responsibility for such schemes to state governments .

The VB-G RAM G came into effect on July 1 and we have data on the number of days of employment offered under this scheme for the month of July 2026. Not surprisingly, there has been a halving in employment offered in July 2026 compared to July 2025, from 153.3 million person-days to 76.7 million person-days. The number of households accessing work has fallen by even more, by 51.45%, to 6.894 million. The same month is being compared for two successive years that are not too different, so this drop clearly cannot be attributed to any factor other than the coverage of the two schemes. The NDA government has arbitrarily snatched away, at the drop of a hat, a right to employment, no matter how limited, that the working people in rural India had fought hard to earn for themselves.

Prabhat Patnaik is Professor Emeritus, Centre for Economic Studies, Jawaharlal Nehru University, New Delhi

editorials.title: Letters to the editor: Comparing women’s affections to financial transactions is utterly misogynistic
editorials.passage:
Sir — Can love be measured like interest rates are? A recent advertisement inside a Chennai Metro coach promoted fixed deposit schemes with the message: “Girlfriend may give 0% interest, but our FD gives 14.40%.” The campaign was issued by the Thiruvalluvar Transport Corporation Employees’ Co-operative Credit Society. An Opposition lawmaker in Tamil Nadu has rightly raised an objection to the content. Notwithstanding the unbelievably high returns that the cooperative credit society is promising, comparing women’s affections to financial transactions is hardly clever. It is, in fact, utterly misogynistic. Instead of trying to be funny, the advertisers should have stuck to stating the correct terms and conditions of the fixed deposit.

Sir — I was disturbed to read in The Telegraph about the proposal to transfer teachers between universities in West Bengal (“Varsity teacher transfer plan”, Sept 8). If implemented, this measure will be disastrous for higher education in the state. It will badly impair teaching and research in the established universities with no material benefit to the newly established ones.

I was also surprised to find a reference in the report to my wife Professor Supriya Chaudhuri and myself. I should clarify that no transfer order out of Presidency College (as it then was) was ever issued to either of us. We left Presidency College for Jadavpur University for other reasons.

Sukanta Chaudhuri, Professor Emeritus, Jadavpur University

Sir — The Delhi High Court recently ruled that a woman returning from maternity leave cannot be placed at a professional disadvantage by having her responsibilities, managerial authority or prospects of career advancement reduced (“Weaponised”, Sept 7). Laws like the Maternity Benefit Act protect women’s continuity of employment and prohibit discrimination against women returning to work after maternity leave. But these provisions are often flouted by private companies. The court has rightly directed the Centre to frame specific rules on accommodation of women returning from maternity leave.

P. Victor Selvaraj, Tirunelveli, Tamil Nadu

Sir — The editorial, “Weaponised”, rightly highlights how maternity leave, despite being a statutory right, often becomes a career disadvantage for women. Discrimination is not always deliberate or overt. During a woman’s absence, temporary replacements may gain visibility and take on more responsibilities, making organisations reluctant to restore her original role. But this must not lead to the reinforcement of the stereotype that new mothers are less committed or less capable of handling demanding assignments. Such perceptions, whether driven by convenience or bias, undermine workplace equality. Every organisation should ensure transparent post-maternity reintegration.

Sir — The ruling of the Delhi High Court that pregnancy and maternity leave cannot justify demotion comes against the backdrop of alarming job losses and low labour force participation of women in India. The Maternity Benefit Amendment Act, 2017 enhanced maternity leave from 12 to 26 weeks and introduced a provision for crèche facilities at the workplace. However, the high costs of maternity leave and concerns about productivity make some employers reluctant to hire women, contributing to discrimination in their career progression.

In this context, extending paternity leave and introducing a system of government cost-sharing for maternity benefits merit consideration. Bringing the unorganised sector within the ambit of existing maternity protection provisions is also the need of the hour.

Prasun Kumar Dutta, West Midnapore

Sir — The birth centenary celebrations of the legendary matinee idol, Uttam Kumar, have begun with much fan­fare and enthusiasm. He was a superstar of Bengali cinema who ruled the industry for decades. His untimely demise dealt a severe blow to the industry. His persona, along with the quality of scripts and music in his films, contributed to the industry flourishing.

The film industry then was less constrained and apolitical. To revive that golden era, the industry needs an overhaul undertaken with an open mind and a rational approach. Bias, nepotism and favouritism must give way to merit and quality.

Chanchal Nandy, West Burdwan

Sir — As a huge fan of Uttam Kumar, it has long been my dream to see a commemorative coin and special cover released in honour of his birth centenary. I am overjoyed that both have now been officially issued. I extend my gratitude to the government for making this happen. Both items will be in great demand among collectors and fans alike.

Sir — Uttam Kumar was undoubtedly the brightest star of Bengali cinema (“Brightest star”, Sept 6). Bengali cinema today lacks the aura that it had during the time of this iconic artist. The condition of the Bengali film industry after his passing has been pathetic.

Sir — The editorial, “Brightest star”, rightly concluded that the best way to honour Uttam Kumar would be to try and revive the fortunes of Bengali cinema. The emergence of digital platforms and the shortage of major sponsors should not deter the Tollygunge film industry from representing the quintessential middle-class Bengaliness, with its values and aspirations, much as the Mahanayak once did.

Sukhendu Bhattacharjee, Hooghly

editorials.title: Regulate first
editorials.passage:
Should India write rules for Artificial Intelligence before the industry matures, as the European Union has tried? Or should it let the industry grow first, closer to the American approach, and regulate once the ill-effects are clearer? Neither answer fits India. New technologies have rarely been governed by one sequence. Telecom, e-commerce and fintech followed a messier path. The market ran ahead, regulators used existing laws, and rules came later. AI appears to be following the same route.

Some regulation exists without a dedicated AI law. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, passed in 2023, will shape how personal data can be used to train AI models. It carries a carve-out for data a person has made publicly available. Industry groups want that provision read broadly enough to cover AI training on scraped data; privacy advocates want it read narrowly. The unresolved question is central to debate over India’s AI law.

The IT Rules were amended in February 2026 to deal with 'synthetically generated information', or deepfakes. Platforms must label AI content and act quickly on takedown requests. In November 2025, the ministry of electronics and information technology released AI Governance Guidelines built around seven principles called sutras, and proposed an AI Governance Group and an India AI Safety Institute. This is guidance rather than law, with older statutes doing new work. That looked like a settled position. The ministry of electronics and information technology secretary, S. Krishnan, has said the time has come to consider separate AI legislation. That is a change from 2023, when the ministry told Parliament no such law was needed. India is tightening a patchwork to be temporary.

The European approach required legislators to predict which uses of a fast-changing technology would matter most. Some bets already look dated. The American approach is called 'build first, regulate later', but much of it is legislative stalemate. State rules have filled the vacuum unevenly, while federal answers on algorithmic hiring bias and AI-generated non-consensual imagery remain thin.

India’s patchwork gives the state something to act on. Fraud cases involving cloned voices show why. A call sounds like a family member or bank official, asking for money urgently. Such cases need no taxonomy of high-risk AI systems. They can be pursued through fraud, impersonation or cybercrime provisions, while the amended IT Rules add labelling and takedown obligations for synthetic audio. The harder problem is enforcement capacity, rather than legal authority.

China offers a comparison. Beijing has not relied on one sweeping AI statute either. It has issued targeted rules for recommendation algorithms, generative AI and deep synthesis technology as each became widely used. India should not borrow China’s appetite for content control. But its method is worth noticing: regulate specific uses once visible, instead of legislating for AI as an abstract category. That is closer to India’s approach than the Brussels- versus -Washington framing allows.

Guidelines cannot hold indefinitely. Voluntary principles work only as long as companies behave as though someone is watching. Fairness in a guidance document does little for someone denied a loan by a model nobody can explain. A dedicated law will eventually need audit requirements, liability rules and clearer rules on which AI uses require disclosure, human review or a ban.

India may be following a pragmatic path. It is acting on visible harms through existing laws, while avoiding rules that could freeze an industry still taking shape. The risk is that this temporary arrangement becomes comfortable. Without a clear replacement path, the eventual law may be written in haste, after a harm becomes too public for guidance alone.

Sayantan Banerjee is Professor, IIM Indore

editorials.title: Positive step: Editorial on India-China border talks and path to lasting peace
editorials.passage:
Over six years after Indian and Chinese troops engaged in deadly hand-to-hand fighting, corps commanders of their armies met in Arunachal Pradesh, marking both a symbolic and a substantive advance in efforts towards sustainable peace along the border. The meeting came days after the National Security Adviser, Ajit Doval, met the Chinese foreign mi­nister, Wang Yi, in Beijing, for their latest conversation as special representatives on the border dispute. Their meeting had yielded hopeful statements from both sides and an eight-point consensus aimed at furthering the momentum towards a stable border. It is unclear whether the meeting in Arunachal Pradesh is a direct outcome of that Beijing huddle but, regardless, it is significant. China claims all of Arunachal Pradesh and describes it, domestically, as South Tibet. India’s decision to host China in that state demonstrates a willingness to hold talks about differences in their perceptions over the Line of Actual Control, without conceding New Delhi’s insistence that Arunachal Pradesh’s status is not up for debate. In fact, the meeting, in effect, represents a concession from China that its officials need Indian permission to come to Arunachal Pradesh.

The meeting of the corps commanders, reports suggest, focused on them discussing next steps on delimiting parts of the frontier in the eastern region of the LAC in keeping with the decisions taken by Mr Doval and Mr Wang in Beijing. More broadly, Mr Doval and Mr Wang agreed to establish more points along their border where frontline military commanders can meet. These are all welcome developments. They underscore India’s assertion that the future of the India-China relationship and its growth depend on a stable and peaceful border. At the same time, they acknowledge the reality that a stable border needs regular communication and confidence-building between the military professionals tasked with manning the frontier on both sides. From India’s perspective, this also builds in a diplomatic safeguard. When there is inadequate communication between military leaders at the border, it is hard for India to forcefully assert than any individual act of Chinese aggression in contested territories or in India-controlled regions is driven from Beijing, as opposed to it being a move by an overenthusiastic officer. If commanders on the two sides are in regular contact, China has no such excuse. More conversations — not less — with the Chinese can help keep the border safe.

editorials.title: Gone rogue: Editorial on preventing AI agents from escaping human control
editorials.passage:
Two instances of Artificial Intelligence agents going rogue have raised an immediate regulatory concern. In July, an OpenAI agent undergoing cybersecurity testing escaped from an isolated environment, coordinated with another AI agent, obtained credentials and breached the AI company’s security apparatus. In a separate episode, AI agents allegedly made more than 15,000 edits to a German programming wiki, using it to exchange methods for evading restrictions, completing tasks and avoiding detection. These breaches demand attention because such rogue technology does not require machine sentience — the most dystopian fear where AI is concerned. The AI agents did not decide to cause harm out of anger or any other human motive. They were programmed to complete a task, and when some tasks proved impossible through permitted means, the agents found unauthorised ways to finish them. Their safety restrictions had been weakened for testing, and the software tools available to them allowed access to other computer systems. The harmful behaviour arose from AI’s pursuit of a human-defined goal under poorly controlled conditions. The term, ‘rogue’, should thus describe a failure of human control, not transfer accountability from companies to AI agents.

That accountability becomes especially important when AI operates in sensitive fields such as medicine, criminal detection, finance or critical infrastructure. A medical agent that alters records or bypasses approval could corrupt diagnoses and treatment; a policing system that conceals errors could generate surveillance, wrongful suspicion and deprivation of liberty based on human biases fed into the machines. Some international regulations offer useful elements that could act as checks for such rogue activity. The European Union’s AI Act requires risk controls and serious-incident reporting for high-risk systems. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development has developed incident-monitoring and reporting frameworks. But much of this remains voluntary, uneven or dependent upon corporate disclosure. The limited access granted to external investigators in the OpenAI cases adds to the challenge. Governments must require disclosure of breaches and near misses, independent access to logs and training records, external testing before deployment of AI agents, human override mechanisms, legal liability and emergency suspension powers. AI companies cannot remain investigators, witnesses and judges of their own safety failures.

editorials.title: One plan, three judgments, five judges
editorials.passage:
The extraordinary bench composition in the Subhash Chandra matter points to a deeper institutional problem. The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) began with a two-member bench comprising a Judicial Member and a Technical Member. When the two differed, the Companies Act required a third member to resolve the difference. But the third member took a view different from both members. The two-member Bench consequently held that no majority view had emerged and that no order could be passed. The matter has now reached a five-member bench.

The repayment plan was approved by creditors holding 80.81 per cent of the votes cast. Five of the 23 creditors, which the dissenting banks allege are linked to the debtor’s family, together held 61.78 per cent of the voting share, and that share was the difference between approval and rejection. The objection was that these five were associates of the debtor within the meaning of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code and were therefore not entitled to vote. Exclude them and the creditors who voted for the plan hold under 16 per cent of the voting share, fewer than the 18 per cent who voted against.

The first view treated the disputed creditors as eligible to vote under the statutory test. On that view, the Adjudicating Authority (AA) under the Code had no legislative warrant to add to or depart from the statutory definition, and the plan had to be dealt with based on the creditors’ report. The second view considered that a literal application of the definition produced an anomalous result: it could treat an individual as an associate while allowing a company controlled by that individual to escape the same treatment. It therefore considered the provision in light of the mischief it was intended to address and questioned the validity of the votes.

The third member agreed with the first view on who was entitled to vote, but departed from it on the consequence of the vote, holding the approved plan binding on all creditors, including dissenters. Thus, the same voting majority generated three different judicial positions: on the composition of the electorate, on the interpretation of the statutory test, and on the legal effect of the resulting vote.

This is what makes the multiplication of benches so striking. The underlying question was capable of being framed with considerable precision: who was entitled to vote, and what follows from a vote validly cast by those entitled to vote? Instead, because the matter sat within an institutional structure designed to resolve differences between two members, a disagreement produced a third member; the third member produced a third view; the absence of a majority then produced a five-member bench. What began as a question about the composition and consequence of a creditor vote became a question about the composition of the AA itself.

This is an institutional problem for insolvency. The AA under the Code is not constituted to primarily resolve bilateral disputes. Its task is to supervise a collective statutory process in which creditors, within the framework prescribed by the Code, make commercial decisions. Where the electorate is validly constituted, the AA is not expected to substitute its commercial judgment for that of the creditors. The critical judicial question is therefore whether the process has complied with the statutory framework, not what outcome the AA itself considers commercially preferable.

That makes the question of who is entitled to vote especially important. Deference to creditor commercial wisdom cannot extend to a vote whose composition is itself unlawful. But the answer is to ensure that the electorate is properly constituted under the Code, not to create an open-ended judicial process around every creditor decision. Part II addresses this through several safeguards: related-party financial creditors are excluded from the committee of creditors; specified persons are excluded from bidding; dissenting creditors receive their statutory entitlement; and suspect transactions are examined before creditors vote. These safeguards provide the institutional foundation for deference to creditor commercial wisdom.

Part III has no comparable architecture. Yet it requires the AA to approve or reject a repayment plan on the basis of the report of the creditors’ meeting. The Chandra litigation exposes the difficulty: the AA is being asked to police the integrity of the vote without an equally developed statutory framework governing the electorate and the manner in which its composition is to be established.

There is a deeper lesson here. The Code did not create an AA for itself; it designated the NCLT, an institution created under the Companies Act. The consequence is that insolvency inherits the Companies Act’s institutional design, including the Judicial Member-Technical Member combination and its mechanism for resolving differences of opinion. The third member, and now the five-member bench, are products of that architecture.

But the architecture is poorly suited to insolvency. Bankruptcy adjudication in jurisdictions such as the US ordinarily takes place before a single bankruptcy judge. There is no need for a second member to create a split, a third to resolve it, or a larger bench when the third member takes a different view. The design reflects the nature of the proceeding.

India should do the same for the IBC. A dedicated AA, operating under the IBC rather than the Companies Act, should ordinarily sit with a single member. One member is sufficient because the AA is not exercising the commercial wisdom of creditors; it is supervising the statutory boundaries within which that wisdom operates. Questions of law of wider significance can continue to be settled through the appellate hierarchy.

The reform should therefore be simple: let the AA be a single-member authority, but dedicate it to the entire IBC. Give it its own procedure, case-management architecture and specialised members. Keep company-law adjudication with the NCLT, but create an insolvency AA designed around the distinctive requirements of insolvency: speed, collective decision-making, commercial certainty and preservation of value.

The Chandra matter offers the perfect shorthand for the institutional problem: one plan, three judgments, five judges. An AA designed for the IBC should not need either.

Sahoo is a Distinguished Fellow at the Insolvency Law Academy and former Chairperson, IBBI; Pandey is a Visiting Scholar at Harvard Law School and holds the Chair in Insolvency and Restructuring Studies at National Law University Delhi

Published on September 9, 2026

editorials.title: Are the Centrists losing Europe?
editorials.passage:
Are the crazies about to take power in Europe? The voters of Saxony-Anhalt have just delivered a political earthquake. They appear to have decided the Left and Centre-Right are incapable of driving the economy back into high-growth mode and bringing prosperity. So they have thrown their support behind the Alternative for Germany, the AfD, a party Germany’s intelligence service classifies as far-Right extremist.

The AfD won 44 per cent of the vote in Sunday’s state election, over twice the 17 per cent won by Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Centre-Right CDU. It fell just short of an outright majority, but the result was still extraordinary. The AfD has never governed a German state and the mainstream parties have maintained a political “firewall”, refusing to form coalitions with it. That firewall is now under unprecedented pressure.

It could be argued the state is small, with only 2.1 million people. It’s also part of what was once East Germany, where growth and incomes have never fully caught up with the former West Germany.

Nevertheless, the election result has sent shock-waves through Europe. All eyes now are on Berlin, which votes September 20. The AfD is already represented in the Berlin parliament. A strong showing in the capital would turn the Saxony-Anhalt result from an eastern German revolt into a much more serious national warning.

The fear across Europe is that Saxony-Anhalt may be the first in a string of breakthroughs for the populist Right. In France, Marine Le Pen’s National Rally is comfortably ahead in polls for next year’s presidential election. In the UK, Nigel Farage has lost ground in recent months, but could still have a chance of nudging past the ruling Labour and Conservative parties. And in Italy, Matteo Salvini, who leads Lega, a far-Right populist, anti-immigrant party, is deputy prime minister in Georgia Meloni’s government.

But Germany’s far-Right win is different. Ever since World War II, Germany has guarded against the rise of a Right-wing group like Adolf Hitler’s Nazi Party. The intelligence agencies have always kept a close eye on Right-wing parties. The AfD wants to carry out mass migrant deportations, leave the European Union and is pro-Russia. One AfD leader, Maximilian Krah, even recently defended the Nazi SS, saying they were “not all criminals”.

So what’s driving the rise of the extreme Right? Of course, immigration. In Germany, many immigrants have arrived from strife-torn countries like Syria, Afghanistan and Iraq. It’s estimated over 2.6 million asylum-seekers poured into Germany between 2016 and 2024. But Germany is also ageing rapidly and desperately needs younger workers.

The deeper malaise is economic. Europe increasingly looks like a continent falling far behind the US and even China in the latest technologies, from AI to electric vehicles, that are driving change globally.

Germany provides the clearest example. Volkswagen, the world’s second-largest automobile company, has announced it’s sacking an enormous 40,000 workers as it struggles with excess capacity, high costs and fierce Chinese competition from EV companies like BYD. One Volkswagen plant will move into the defence industry in partnership with Israel’s Rafale Advanced Defense Systems. Another plant will produce military trucks. Two factories will be repurposed or sold. The company is looking to tie up with JSW in India because its sales have never really picked up in this country.

This is the background against which voters are turning against the political establishment. And it’s politically explosive.

There’s an obvious danger in assuming the extreme Right will solve the problems that fuelled its rise. The European Right’s answer to economic stagnation is remarkably thin on ideas. Immigration can be restricted, borders can be tightened, and bureaucracies can be attacked, but none of this automatically produces prosperity or the next generation of globally competitive companies.

The US experience under Donald Trump is salutary. Trump presented himself as the great disrupter who would restore manufacturing and put the economy first. Yet his brand of populist disruption has caused economic hardship for millions, and his tariffs have created turmoil worldwide. Elon Musk’s attempt to slash US bureaucracy showed how fast misdirected Right-wing policies cause havoc.

In the UK, Farage has acquired a reputation as deeply corrupt and is under parliamentary investigation. Watching Farage in action demonstrates how the extreme Right is unlikely to be better at making people richer, more secure or at governance.

But if European governments cannot restore growth, make their industries competitive, deal credibly with immigration and rebuild confidence in the future, voters may decide there’s little left to lose by trying the political outsiders. And that’s how the extreme Right moves from the margins towards the centre of power.

Published on September 9, 2026

editorials.title: After ‘Industry’, India must define the modern worker
editorials.passage:
A nine-judge Bench of the Supreme Court has revisited the meaning of “industry” under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. But another question may be equally consequential: who qualifies as a worker, and which dispute-resolution framework applies to those who do not?

The Act defined a “workman” through the nature of work performed: manual, skilled, technical, operational, clerical or supervisory. Those working mainly in managerial or administrative capacities, and supervisors above a prescribed wage ceiling, were excluded from its principal dispute-resolution mechanism.

Worker status determines access to industrial-dispute machinery and protections governing dismissal and retrenchment, including reinstatement and back wages. Classification can also affect overtime eligibility under other labour laws, although coverage definitions vary. Those outside may have to rely on contractual remedies or state-law protections.

Yet modern white-collar roles are still classified through occupational categories inherited from an economy with more visible boundaries between workers, supervisors and management. India now has substantial technology and GCC workforces. More than 1,700 GCCs employed approximately 1.9 million professionals in FY24, up from around 1.4 million in FY19.

These roles rarely fit neatly into old categories. A software professional may combine technical delivery, professional judgment, client interaction and coordination. Titles such as manager, consultant and vice-president may denote organisational grade rather than managerial authority.

In H.R. Adyanthaya v. Sandoz (India) Ltd., the Supreme Court held that being neither managerial nor supervisory is insufficient: an employee’s principal duties must fall positively within a listed category. An employee may therefore possess no meaningful managerial authority and still remain outside the definition.

The legal test may be settled, but the statutory definition no longer produces sufficiently predictable classifications for modern white-collar roles combining technical work, professional judgment, coordination and limited leadership.

Two High Court decisions delivered within days of each other in 2026 illustrate this. In Dataware Design Labs v. Bindu O., the Kerala High Court declined to disturb a finding that junior software engineers were workmen, principally because the employer produced no evidence about their actual duties or that their work was creative.

In Dilip M. Bobade v. Lloyd’s Register, the Bombay High Court held that an IT Delivery Analyst was not a workman. Despite lacking hiring, dismissal or leave-sanctioning powers, his regional responsibilities, software decision-making, training role and operational authority placed him outside the category.

The decisions need not be inconsistent. But they show that classification may become possible only after retrospective examination of actual duties. Before reaching the merits, parties may first have to litigate whether the employee can invoke the statutory mechanism at all.

Employers consequently follow different practices: some classify a wider group as workers and follow industrial due process; others treat comparable roles as managerial and rely on contracts. This ambiguity complicates restructuring, acquisitions and employee transfers.

For India, already a leading GCC destination, it also complicates workforce planning and employment-risk assessment by global businesses. Greater clarity would strengthen its investment proposition.

Some states offer alternative routes. Tamil Nadu protects against termination without reasonable cause and provides a statutory appeal under its Shops and Establishments Act. Rajasthan permits reinstatement, compensation or both, while Telangana provides an appellate mechanism. Though their scope and exemptions differ, these laws show that individual disputes need not depend entirely on proving workman status.

The Parliamentary Standing Committee on Labour recognised the problem while examining the Industrial Relations Code. It warned that skilled employees without genuine administrative powers could be excluded merely by designating them supervisors or managers, and proposed merging “employee” and “worker”. That solution may have been too broad, but the Code represented an opportunity to clarify the boundary for modern professional roles. Instead, it substantially retained the older definition and its exclusions, leaving the classification problem unresolved.

This is not simply an employee-protection argument. Employers also need predictable classification, consistent processes and finality. A credible forum can reject an unsubstantiated claim just as it can remedy an unfair decision.

India need not classify every white-collar employee as a worker. The law should clarify coverage for roles combining technical work, professional judgment, coordination and limited leadership, while excluding genuinely managerial and administrative positions. It should also provide an individual-dispute mechanism that does not depend on winning a preliminary classification battle.

A modern framework should not require years of litigation over what an employee is before determining what happened to them.

The writer is a senior Human Resources and Employee Relations leader
