editorials.title: Instead of chasing GDP growth, India must redesign its broken ladder of upward mobility
editorials.passage:
India’s leaders must find systemic solutions to the country’s employment problems. The economy is not creating enough good jobs for young people, even if more were to pursue higher education and the examination system functioned smoothly. More technology to fix the examination system will not solve the deeper problem of the economy.

Moreover, there is increasing evidence that use of more technology and AI will worsen India’s unemployment crisis. While it may be unclear whether AI will create more jobs ultimately, it is sufficiently clear that inequality will rise during the transition, increasing further the distance between “haves” and “have nots”.

India’s youth need a ladder to climb to reach their aspirations. They want gainful employment, and to earn enough to secure their own and their families’ futures. The economy has not provided them a good ladder to climb from where they are, to the higher floors above where they can live well and safely. The ladder provided so far is both broken and misaligned. It is missing the lower rungs necessary for those who do not have the means to reach the higher rungs of education from which they can climb further. And those who can climb up find there is nothing up there for them.

For many decades now, solutions for the jobless growth of the economy have been to grow GDP faster, skill more youth, and build institutions of higher education. The principal reform of the economy that has being pursued, fruitlessly, is to move more people out of agriculture, with the hope that they will find employment in manufacturing, services, and in urban areas. Most jobs in those sectors are insecure and do not pay well. The young are losing hope in the “ache din” promised in 2014 by Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

The State of Working India 2026 report compiled by Azim Premji University shows that the real earnings growth of graduate men, who are already employed, has declined by 0.1% per annum since 2017. The Economic Survey 2024-’25 reveals that over 50% of Indian graduates are classified as unemployed; and that only 8% of those employed are in jobs that match their qualification.

Economists worry that India’s unorganised and informal sector is too large. They want the formal and organised sector to grow larger. However, jobs in the formal sector are becoming fewer with firms deploying more technology and AI to improve productivity. In fact, India’s IT firms, who were large providers of jobs for India’s graduates, are now using more AI themselves and reducing employment.

Moreover, contractualisation of work in the formal sector, with the replacement of full-time employees with employees on short term contracts – to provide the firms with “hiring and firing flexibility” to keep down their costs, has resulted in wage compression. The Economic Survey estimates that the real (inflation adjusted) earnings of workers have fallen by 6.4% between 2017-’18 and 2023-’24.

Contractualisation of work has other harmful effects for the economy. Workers lose social security; and they are deprived of opportunities to continue learning on the job and upgrading their skills. This adds further burdens on the government for resources for social security, when it is already under pressure from its economic advisers to cut back its expenditure, and not increase taxes on corporations and the rich because that will reduce their incentives to invest more in their enterprises, to install more automation and AI to improve their productivity and reduce employment further!

Let us apply “systems thinking” to the economy. To connect the many fixes applied, and understand why they backfire on each other, and slow down the creation of jobs and dampen income growth. Some of these fixes are flexibility for employers to adjust employment costs; more AI to improve performance in all sectors; reduced taxes on corporations to encourage more investment; reduction of government borrowing to make more room for private borrowing; reduction of governments’ health and education budgets and encouragement of private enterprises in health and education (who will employ people on contract, use more AI, etc. to improve their internal efficiencies).

Pushing harder on each of these seemingly good fixes is jamming income growth. Since incomes and social security are not growing faster than inflation, consumption is slowing, and investments are not forthcoming, though the government is pleading for more.

A nation is a socio-economic system sustained by its natural environment. The modern model of an economy is a system designed to enable more efficient extraction of natural resources and exploitation of human beings’ labor and intelligence. This is not sustainable. For one, the natural environment is running out of resources to feed greed for economic growth. Also, with the masses not earning enough, who will pay for the products and services of technology (and AI) empowered enterprises?

Policy makers must return to the drawing board and redesign the earnings ladder. Economists must reimagine “work”. Especially the work done within families, and the work that is done “informally”, outside formal, factory-like settings. Also, the unpaid, or insufficiently paid work that women (and men) do in “social” enterprises like families and communities to provide care for others. It may not contribute much to the money-measured GDP that work in “economic” enterprises does. But it is essential work for society’s sustenance.

The contradictions between prudent management of the economy, provision of care services, and employment of more women are starkly visible in India. Approximately 4 million women are employed as ASHA workers, anganwadi workers, and anganwadi worker helpers to provide medical care and care of children in communities. Their approximate, average monthly earnings are: ASHAs Rs 3,000 to Rs 8,000, anganwadi workers Rs 4,500, and anganwadi helpers Rs 3,000. The exact amounts are not important: the sums are so small. They have been protesting across the country for more wages, but central and state governments say they cannot afford to pay them more.

In summary, more GDP cannot be the solution for increasing employment and incomes until the employment elasticity of the Indian economy is improved (ie, the numbers of good jobs generated with each unit of GDP). Economists estimate that the GDP of an unreformed economy will have to grow at least 8.5% per annum for the next decade, starting now to provide enough jobs, whereas with difficulty it is growing around 6%.

An unreformed economic structure, with more privatisation, can no longer provide decent jobs with sustainable income growth for Indian citizens. Exporting human beings abroad to earn and remit money home to sustain their families and the Indian economy is not a dignified solution for a country that wishes to be seen as a beacon of wisdom and compassion in the world.

India’s economy must be reformed. It must return to the vision of “poorna swaraj” – equal political, social, and economic opportunities for all citizens, whatever their castes or religions. That is its “tryst with destiny”, that “India ie Bharat” set out for on August 15, 1947. Our policymakers lost their way when they began to pursue targets of GDP growth.

Arun Maira is the author of Reimagining India’s Economy: The Road to a More Equitable Society.

editorials.title: AfD’s rise in Germany indicates ‘liberal democracies’ have run their course
editorials.passage:
The result of a provincial election has triggered an apocalyptic reaction among the mainstream political parties in Germany and pearl clutching across the liberal establishment in Europe. The Alternative for Germany (AfD), a nationalist party that Germany’s domestic spy agency classified as a ‘right-wing extremist’ outfit last year, has surged to first place during polls in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, winning 39 seats of the 83-member state parliament (or 44 per cent of the vote), falling three seats short of an absolute majority.

Headless chickens look more composed in comparison.

In Berlin, the political class has greeted the democratic choice of the electorate as a cosmic malfunction. German chancellor Friedrich Merz said the AfD’s victory has shaken his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) “to its very foundations” and would have “consequences” reaching well beyond the region. “It is an election result we cannot simply move past as if nothing happened,” he said Monday. “It is the most severe election defeat the CDU has suffered in years, indeed in decades.”

The Brandmauer — a political firewall whereby German outfits of all stripes coalesce to prevent ‘ultra-nationalist’ AfD from joining ruling coalitions — has given rise to strange bedfellows and a game of musical chairs. While mainstream parties contorted themselves into an alphabet soup of ideologically incompatible coalitions just to erect a moral barricade against a popular choice, German voters interpreted it as a cancellation of their mandate.

Apparently, scolding disgruntled voters didn’t work. Now, confronted with the revelation that treating the voting public like disobedient children didn’t win them over, Merz’s CDU or coalition partner Social Democrats (SPD) are sounding bewildered.

It mirrors the hysteria across the rest of the continent. From Brussels to Paris, liberal editorialists and eurocrats are hyperventilating, issuing hand-wringing declarations about the imminent collapse of Western civilisation. Amid all the finger-wagging and moral panic, Europe’s centrist elites cannot seem to figure out the root causes of voter dissatisfaction.

The entire old continent is suffering from the same affliction that Germany is showing the latest symptoms of. Europe’s ‘cordon sanitaire’, its own version of the hard-right firewall, is cracking under pressure as the ‘nationalists’ are emerging as a dominant force and reshaping the continent’s political landscape — both within the European Union and at the national level. They are rapidly transitioning from fringe opposition to executive power.

In the European Parliament, three hard-right factions collectively command 196 seats, forming the second-largest bloc. Right-wing outfits are leading ruling coalitions in Italy and the Czech Republic, and serving as junior partners in governments across Finland, Croatia, Slovakia, and Sweden. Their influence pervades even where they do not govern directly, as evidenced by the Freedom Party’s first-place finish in Austria, Geert Wilders’s strong showing in the Netherlands, and Marine Le Pen’s enduring dominance in France. Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni has further reinforced this shift.

Given Germany’s Nazi past, for purely historical reasons the rise of AfD has created the greatest churn. The party has been accused of xenophobia, ethnonationalism and antisemitism in its ideological framework and political culture.

The AfD, which has evolved from a Eurosceptic outfit to Germany’s biggest opposition force, has positioned itself against what it frames as an elite, out-of-touch, and increasingly ‘woke’ mainstream establishment. Young men are routinely cited as a demographic that feels alienated or censored by progressive identity politics, making them receptive to the AfD’s countercultural, anti-establishment messaging, which the party amplifies through social media platforms like TikTok.

Instead of throwing labels, however, it might be worth exploring the fundamentals behind AfD’s meteoric rise despite its problematic ‘vision’ for Germany. It is my contention that the rise of the hard right across Europe — from Britain’s Reform UK to France’s National Rally — and also the United States led by the redoubtable Donald Trump of the MAGA cult, represents the formal death of liberal democracy – the dominant ideological framework since the Second World War.

Before I expand on my argument, let me run you through AfD’s ‘vision’ for Germany that may represent a thematic pattern in voter behaviour. The AfD envisions a radical restructuring of the German state, pivoting away from the country’s post-war liberal consensus towards right-wing populism and cultural homogeneity.

At the core of the AfD’s plan is a drastic overhaul of immigration, asylum, and integration policies. The party calls for “remigration”, an ambiguous term that hints at Trump-style mass deportation of undocumented immigrants, asylum seekers and non-citizens, alongside the abolition of the constitutional right to asylum.

The party has proposed radically altering the German education system by introducing segregated classes for refugee children who would be removed from mainstream German schools. The curriculum will have “less of Nazi past and more on the periods of German history before World War One and Two to instill national pride.”

In foreign policy, a cornerstone of the AfD’s policy involves a dramatic pivot away from the NATO consensus, seeking instead to hew Germany much closer to Russia. The AfD envisions a strategic partnership, demanding the resumption of cheap Russian energy imports which they argue is vital for the survival of German industry. This pro-Russian alignment is advocated with Euroscepticism and a referendum on Germany’s exit (Dexit).

Culturally, the AfD champions a ‘Germany First’ doctrine centred on a dominant traditional German culture. In its manifesto, the party has rejected multiculturalism and maintained that “Islam does not belong to Germany.”

The AfD opposes progressive social movements, seeking to purge ‘gender ideology’ and diversity initiatives from public life. To address demographic decline, they propose offering financial incentives to native German families to have more children rather than relying on immigration.

Finally, its economic policies favour a free market with reduced bureaucracy but heavily curtailed social welfare benefits for non-citizens. The party dismisses consensus on climate change and strongly opposes Germany’s green energy transition, advocating for the continued use of coal, combustion engines, and nuclear energy.

In short, AfD’s Germany would reject multiculturalism and permissive borders in favour of a culturally homogeneous, isolationist state with strong ties to Moscow. If the AfD is within striking distance of power, it must be admitted that the German populace — a large majority of them anyway — has bought into its core narrative, that the establishment is an indistinguishable, elite uniparty conspiring against the will of the people.

This brings me to the fundamental problem with liberal democracies such as post-Cold War United States or Europe that are underpinned by liberal hegemony – the ideological framework championed by the US that emerged as a superpower in the aftermath of the Second World War. The US, flush with power and convinced of its exceptionalism, fostered an open international economy, globalisation, relaxed immigration policies and formidable liberal institutions as it went about casting the world in its image.

In his book, The Great Delusion: Liberal Dreams and International Realities, American political scientist and theorist John Mearsheimer writes, “Liberal hegemony is an ambitious strategy in which a state aims to turn as many countries as possible into liberal democracies like itself while also promoting an open international economy and building international institutions. In essence, the liberal state seeks to spread its own values far and wide.”

Mearsheimer predicts that when it runs against nationalism, “liberal hegemony will not achieve its goals, and its failure will inevitably come with huge costs.” To the professor of ‘offensive realism’, “nationalism is an enormously powerful political ideology” that “revolves around the division of the world into a wide variety of nations, which are formidable social units, each with a distinct culture.”

Mearsheimer writes that “there is no question that liberalism and nationalism can coexist, but when they clash, nationalism almost always wins… Liberals believe everyone has the same rights, regardless of which country they call home. Nationalism is a particularist ideology from top to bottom, which means it does not treat rights as inalienable. In practice, the vast majority of people around the globe do not care greatly about the rights of individuals in other countries.”

While this explains the power structure of nation-states where nationalist tendencies eventually trump liberal impulses, at an ideological level, liberalism’s egalitarian structure is at odds with evolutionary survival strategies.

I must stress here that I am referring to classical liberalism that evolved from a need to focus on limiting government power, protecting private property, ensuring free markets, and securing civil rights like free speech and religious freedom. The trouble arose when liberalism gave way to progressivism since the late 20th century, expanding beyond economic equality to focus heavily on cultural and social issues: emphasising diversity, LGBT rights, cosmopolitanism, and dismantling systemic inequalities related to race and gender.

While this transition was inevitable, progressivism and neoliberalism created profound economic and cultural changes that alienated large segments of the population, setting the stage for a populist backlash. While the US-led West championed a globalised economy – where manufacturing jobs moved overseas or immigrants were let in — it left in its wake groups such as working and middle classes that felt the political establishment rooted in centre-left or centre-right were not representing or acting on their concerns.

Simultaneously, the rapid advancement of progressive social values triggered a cultural backlash. Progressive liberalism embraces a cosmopolitan, open-borders mindset, viewing national identity as fungible. Working-class citizens whose identities are deeply tied to their nation, religion, and local communities perceive it as an attack on their way of life.

This, too, is inescapable because the in-group/out-group framework determines how we construct our sense of self, and our self-esteem is tied to the status and success of the groups we identify with. An added layer of complexity in liberal democracies is that multicultural policies end up encouraging parallel societies and community segregation rather than a shared national identity or social cohesion.

In the German context, it is not surprising that the 2015 refugee crisis was the catalyst for the AfD’s transformation from a fringe group into a powerful nationalist force. AfD frames immigration not just as an economic burden but as an existential threat to German cultural homogeneity and seeks “remigration” to preserve what it views as traditional identity.

Former German chancellor Angela Merkel has expressed shock at AfD’s win, saying it has “broken her heart”.

That’s a bit rich, considering that Merkel’s signature open-border policy is widely thought to have contributed to AfD’s rise. Her suspension of the Dublin Regulation and the subsequent arrival of over a million undocumented migrants inexorably altered the German social fabric.

In her autobiography, Merkel had acknowledged the problem, admitting that her “opening of Germany’s borders to tens of thousands of refugees and migrants from Syria, Lebanon, Afghanistan, the Balkans and Africa in September 2015 was a turning point of her years in office because it was and remains bitterly divisive.”

The rise of AfD or nationalist political parties on both sides of the Atlantic, therefore, is an inevitable turn of history, representing the fact that liberal democracy as an idea has run its course.

(Views expressed in the above piece are personal. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: The West is exporting its problems — again
editorials.passage:
Western countries have a bad habit of burdening developing countries with undesirable consequences of their economic and environmental policies. At first, they sent their toxic waste to some developing countries, a process that still continues. Thereafter, they moved polluting industries to them, even as they lost part of their own manufacturing base. Now, Western countries, led by the United States, have reached a third stage —sending illegal immigrants or asylum seekers, not to their home countries but to third countries.

Most international conventions, promoted by Western countries, require that illegal immigrants are sent back to their home countries provided their safety would not be endangered there. But they ignore these norms themselves. Ironically, they are always in the forefront of accusing the Global South and some other states of flouting human rights. Meanwhile, the US arrogates to itself the right to issue reports on the human rights situations of other countries, including on freedom of religion, expression and the treatment of minorities.

This third stage, led by the United States under President Donald Trump, came into focus again recently. This was because of the harrowing accounts in sections of the Western media that around 1,200 mainly South American immigrants to the US had been deported to two African states — Liberia and Equatorial Guinea. Significantly, European countries are attempting to follow Trump’s example. These processes, taken together, show that these advanced countries still retain colonial approaches and mind-sets.

The US took pride in being a country which opened its doors to the persecuted. A plaque next to the Statue of Liberty contains lines of the poet Emma Lazarus that was once taught to every American child: ‘Give me your tired, your poor/ Your huddled masses yearning to breathe free …I lift my lamp beside the golden door’. This message of hope was really directed to Europe, for it was not until 1965 that the US effectively opened doors to immigrants from other parts of the world. It was also generous in giving asylum to those who entered illegally.

Under the Trump administration those days have become a distant, demeaning past. The dispatch of illegal immigrants to third countries sometimes bypass court orders which have resisted the return of asylum seekers to their home countries where they are likely to be harmed demonstrates these attitudes.

Some human rights groups estimate that there are by now 35 countries that have signed confidential agreements with the US to accept those who have reached it illegally. The overwhelming majority of these countries are impoverished and have difficulties in resisting US pressures or threats that can include the imposition of tariffs. There is little doubt that they are also financially rewarded in one way or another. The third country deals are of different kinds. Some allow the deportees to apply for asylum in these countries while others allow them to remain in special facilities for specific periods of time. After that, they face an uncertain future.

The countries with which the US has these confidential agreements have increased exponentially during Trump’s second term. From 3 in his first term, they have now gone up to 35. They include 13 in Africa, including some such as the Central African Republic and South Sudan, which are witnessing ongoing civil strife. 15 South American and Caribbean states have also entered into such agreements. Interestingly, there are reports that a few European countries are also receiving these deportees from the US. While some sections of the US media and US human rights NGOs have critically reported on these third country deportations, the State Department has supported them as lawful. This is not surprising, for it can hardly do otherwise because one of Trump’s major electoral planks was removing illegal immigrants in one way or another from the US. It is for the American judicial system to decide on the legality of Trump administration’s policies, but they certainly erode the US's self-projection as a humane society.

The US example on third country deportations has now ‘inspired’ European countries to follow suit. The European Parliament agreed in June this year that illegal immigrants in EU countries could be sent to ‘hubs’ in third countries to be held in detention there. Five EU countries—Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece—entered into an agreement on September 4 to establish detention hubs for illegal migrants in third countries. It has been reported that they have begun negotiations with Rwanda on setting up ‘detention hubs’.

As is usual with European countries, they are trying to project that they will respect human rights and international conventions but basically, they are going the US way. These countries are also projecting that their decision will be a disincentive against human trafficking. An end to this terrible criminal business, like an end to narcotics and the illegal arms trade, lies in improving the lives of the peoples of the Global South through a cooperative partnership between the advanced countries and the Global South. This will involve a huge transfer of resources and technologies from the advanced world to the Global South. This is something the advanced world has never been willing to do. Indeed, they have never, as a group, redeemed the pledge they made to transfer 0.7% of their GDP to developing countries. This pledge was made as far back as 1970 in the UNGA.

Significantly, Britain had an agreement with Rwanda in 2022 to set up a ‘detention centre’. This became a hot and divisive political issue. It reached the courts, and the Supreme Court ruled in 2023 that Rwanda was not a safe country to send asylum seekers to detention centres there. It did not, however, find that sending ‘illegal’ migrants in Britain to third country detention centres was inherently illegal! Basically, the EU is now going along with this principle. What is being ignored is that sending illegal migrants to a third country where they have no roots and family is cruel. It is akin to the British practice during colonial times of sending indentured labour to countries which were alien and from where it was virtually impossible for them to return. While Britain abandoned the idea of third country detention centres in 2024, it is now being revived. There are reports that it is negotiating with foreign countries to set these up.

No one can ever defend the evils and criminality of human trafficking which leads to a great deal of illegal migration. Human trafficking has to be fought. All countries also have a right to take effective steps to stop illegal migration and also attempt to send them back to their home countries. However, what the West, led by the US, is now doing by sending them to third-country detention centres should not be acceptable to the Global South even if a large number of its countries are being arm-twisted or seduced by the advanced states to accept them.

(The writer is a former Indian diplomat who served as India’s Ambassador to Afghanistan and Myanmar, and as secretary, the Ministry of External Affairs. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: India’s Dollar Economy (Part 3)—Rs 50 Lakh Cr 'Flee' with Dollar-Millionaires!
editorials.passage: In the first episode of our trilogy on India’s Dollar Economy, we examined the highly curious, oxymoron-like phenomenon of “Zero Net FDI” in the world’s fastest growing large economy. We discovered that the “zero” was a somewhat problematic half-truth, but not a disaster. Fresh Inward FDI (Foreign Direct Investment) is at record highs, but it’s not keeping pace with GDP growth. It’s also counter-balanced by two opposing forces—huge outflows of investable dollars by foreign and domestic companies. So, the picture is awfully grey, encouraging and distressing in about equal proportions. As against this, our second episode, on the legal protections given to foreign investors, showed a severely black/white portrait. The Indian government had devised a 2016 Model Business Investment Treaty (BIT) Framework, leaving the foreign investor vulnerable and disarmed against whimsical taxation and unfair policy changes.Almost all our treaties—over EIGHTY—with critical trading partners were scrapped; and the aggrieved countries are unwilling to conclude fresh treaties under the new norms. Independent estimates showed a gut-wrenching 30 percent fall in FDI caused by this unilateral—some would call “brazen”—treaty action by India.And now, in this third and final piece of our trilogy, we turn our gaze towards ordinary people and their “dollar actions”. This is the story of how Indian citizens and non-resident Indians (NRIs)—i.e., people in flesh and blood, not inorganic/fictitious “legal persons” like corporations—are impacting India’s Dollar Economy. India’s Dollar Economy (Part 1): Net FDI Fell to Zero – Yeah, It’s True!People influence dollar inflows in two ways. One, by moving them in and out of their bank accounts. And two, by moving their bodies and families in and out of India, principally by emigrating and taking their wealth to another country.The only way Indian residents can remit dollars is via a Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS) which allows each one of us to send $250,000 every year to travel to foreign shores, educate our children, give gifts to overseas relatives, get medical treatment, or whatever. So, if you are a family of four living in India, and have Rs 10 crore to spare, you can remit or spend $1 million every year!LRS outflows have grown six-fold over the last decade, from about $5 billion to nearly $30 billion last year. Is that a suspicious surge? Mercifully not. Most of the money—about 60 percent—is spent on foreign travel, which is a hugely aspirational quest, even for simple middle-class families. Predictably, education comes next, with about 20 percent used there. The rest is spread over gifts, medical treatment, and investments in property and financial assets. All of this is rational behaviour as urban Indian families get wealthier. Thankfully then, the LRS track raises no alarm.Now to the dollars that “physically” accompany emigrating Indian residents. The most precise demographic quantity is Indians renouncing their citizenship.The total registered renunciations are nearly 1.6 million over the last decade. But it would be erroneous to use this as a proxy for emigration since the final cut of the umbilical cord with “home” usually comes after several years of living away.Another estimate, much fuzzier, shows a net decadal increase of 2.5 million in the stock of Indian-born people living abroad from 2015. Since many may have also returned or died in this decade, demographers estimate that over 5 million people may have emigrated, at an average rate of about 500,000 every year over the decade. But to estimate the wealth they could have taken with them is a mighty challenge.About 2 million were students. Another 2 million were skilled professionals and their families. Half a million small business owners may also have migrated. Most of them are likely to have left behind their family house and relatives, i.e. wealth that did not migrate with them. Clearly, none of these people are thought to have taken sacksful of dollars with them. What’s more, many would have improved their economic means in foreign lands. If anything, they could be principal contributors to the swelling stream of over $100 billion that are steadily being sent to India by overseas Indians, year after year. So, this emigration stream is not a huge dollar burden on the country.India’s Dollar Economy (Part 2)—Why Did Rs 20 Lakh Cr ($230 bn) Flee BIT by BIT?Now to the most nettlesome category, i.e., High Net Worth (HNI) households. Because if a household with $50-100 million of domestic wealth moves abroad, the probability that eventually over half this wealth will also get sucked away to the “new home country” is quite high. Is there a way to make a scientific guesstimate?Henley/New World Wealth’s 2025 report claims that 3,500 Indian millionaires, worth $26.2 billion, emigrated in 2025. This is the most “validated” data point we can work with. A simple division yields a critical norm, i.e. each of these departing millionaires must have had an average wealth of $7.5 million.If 3,500 dollar-millionaires left India in 2025, do we have an estimate for the total departures over the last decade? Yes, there’s popular consensus that the number could be 50,000, including negligible emigration during the COVID years. Now, if we blindly multiply 50,000 by $7.5 million, we hit our “quick estimate” of $375 billion of wealth owned by this cohort.Such wealthy people are not expected to “clear the stables” in their motherland. Most would want to retain a house, business, or other assets in India.If we make a reasonable assumption that 60 percent is eventually sucked out, and 40 percent stays within India, we have a defendable proxy, i.e. about $200-225 billion of millionaire wealth has, or soon will, “flee” from India, along with its owners.This is a sobering reality! Because these $200-225 billion are EQUITY capital in the hands of the migrants. Even by a conservative debt:equity standard of 2:1, it adds up to over half a trillion dollars of investable capital. That’s nearly Rs 50 lakh crore! What if this was invested in India, and not in Dubai/Singapore/Europe/America/Wherever? That’s the ugly question beguiling India’s Dollar Economy.India's Cautious Approach to BITs Isn't the Only Reason FDI is Falling
